sections.heading: What are the symptoms of type 2 diabetes and how does it develop?
sections.body:
Many people with type 2 diabetes have no symptoms at first, and any signs can build slowly over years. The NHS lists feeling very tired, needing to pee more, constant thirst and unintended weight loss as the most common symptoms. Other possible signs are blurred vision, wounds that heal slowly, and genital itching or repeated thrush.

Because symptoms can be mild or missing, some people are found to have the condition during tests for something else. The NHS describes prediabetes as blood glucose levels that are higher than normal but not high enough for a diagnosis of diabetes. MedlinePlus explains that the pancreas at first makes extra insulin to make up for the body's cells not responding normally to it. Over time the body cannot make enough insulin, and blood glucose levels rise.

sections.heading: How is type 2 diabetes diagnosed, and what do check-ups involve?
sections.body:
A GP can usually diagnose type 2 diabetes with a blood test and a urine test. Guidance also uses HbA1c blood test results in diagnosis. After diagnosis, NICE says there is a thorough check-up every year, called the annual review. The review looks at complications and at whether treatment is working, and includes blood pressure, blood sugar and eye checks.

It can also include a blood test for kidney function and a urine test for kidney disease. If kidney disease is found, treatment can be given to stop it getting worse. A foot check looks at the risk of foot ulcers and at loss of feeling from nerve damage. A foot check is needed even when no changes to the feet have been noticed. Eye screening is usually a photograph of the back of the eye, taken to look for diabetic retinopathy, and it is often arranged separately from the annual review.

sections.heading: What treatments are used for type 2 diabetes?
sections.body:
The NHS describes treatment as lifestyle changes first, then medicines. Lifestyle steps include regular physical activity, losing weight for people who are overweight, stopping smoking and limiting alcohol. A medicine called metformin is usually offered first.

The NHS page notes that an SGLT2 inhibitor, which lets extra sugar leave the body in urine, is often given alongside metformin to people without other serious conditions. A weekly injection of a GLP-1 agonist may be offered to some people, such as those with a history of heart disease or with obesity, when other treatments are not enough. Other tablets such as gliclazide, sitagliptin or pioglitazone are also used.

sections.heading: Can type 2 diabetes go into remission, and when is insulin needed?
sections.body:
The NHS says insulin is prescribed for type 2 diabetes if other diabetes medicines no longer keep blood glucose within a healthy range. Diabetes UK notes that some people can manage type 2 diabetes through healthy eating, being more active or losing weight.

The NHS England Path to Remission Programme offers a low-calorie total diet replacement plan, using soups and shakes, to eligible people in England who have type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity. Research cited by NHS England found that almost half of those on a low-calorie diet reached remission of their type 2 diabetes after one year. The NHS warns against very strict low-calorie diets without medical advice, especially for people taking insulin or other diabetes medicines.

sections.heading: What complications can type 2 diabetes cause, and when should someone get help?
sections.body:
Over time, high blood sugar can damage the blood vessels, nerves, eyes, kidneys, feet and gums. The NHS lists damage that can contribute to coronary heart disease and stroke, foot ulcers and infections that may sometimes lead to amputation, sight problems such as diabetic retinopathy, kidney problems and gum disease. The NHS says diabetes can reduce the blood supply to the feet and cause a loss of feeling. It also says that controlling blood sugar and having regular check-ups is the best way to lower the risk of complications.

Very high blood glucose can lead to emergencies called diabetic ketoacidosis, when ketones build up in the blood, and HHS. The NHS says both can be life threatening. For signs such as confusion, drowsiness, breathlessness or vomiting with high blood glucose, the NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E. For tingling, numbness, constipation or diarrhoea that could signal nerve damage, the NHS advises contacting a GP or diabetes nurse. Blisters or cracked skin on the feet and worsening vision are also reasons to seek non-urgent advice, through a GP appointment. NHS inform says a hot, red, swollen foot, new skin damage or new pain needs urgent contact with a podiatrist or GP, or NHS 111.

sections.heading: Living with type 2 diabetes: eating, activity and daily checks
sections.body:
UK guidance suggests a varied diet with plenty of fruit, vegetables, wholegrains such as wholemeal bread and oats, and pulses such as chickpeas and lentils. The NHS notes that having diabetes increases the harmful effects of smoking. The NHS says a free education course should be offered within a year of diagnosis.

The NHS advises checking the feet every day, with a yearly foot check by a clinician. NHS Wales says people taking insulin for type 2 diabetes need to tell the DVLA, because of the risk of low blood sugar. NHS England says contacting the DVLA may be needed if diabetes causes health problems or if there are low blood sugar episodes, known as hypos.

faqs.q: Can type 2 diabetes go into remission?
faqs.a: Remission is possible for some people, according to NHS England. Its Path to Remission Programme offers a low-calorie total diet replacement plan to eligible people in England with type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity. Research cited by NHS England found that almost half of those on a low-calorie diet reached remission after one year.

faqs.q: How is type 2 diabetes different from type 1?
faqs.a: In type 2 diabetes the pancreas does not make enough insulin, or the body's cells do not react to it. In type 1 diabetes the pancreas does not produce any insulin. One source adds that type 1 is an autoimmune condition, while type 2 is mainly influenced by lifestyle factors and genetics.

faqs.q: Does everyone with type 2 diabetes need insulin?
faqs.a: Treatment usually starts with lifestyle changes and metformin. The NHS says insulin is prescribed if other diabetes medicines no longer keep blood glucose within a healthy range. Diabetes UK notes that some people can manage type 2 diabetes through healthy eating, being more active or losing weight.

faqs.q: Can someone have type 2 diabetes without symptoms?
faqs.a: Yes, many people have no symptoms at first, and signs can build slowly over years. Some people are found to have it during tests for something else. A GP can usually diagnose it with a blood test and a urine test.

faqs.q: When is type 2 diabetes an emergency?
faqs.a: The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E for signs such as confusion, drowsiness, breathlessness or vomiting with high blood glucose, as these could be DKA or HHS. Both can be life threatening. For tingling, numbness, cracked skin on the feet or worsening vision, the NHS suggests non-urgent advice from a GP or diabetes nurse.

keyFacts.label: Usual first medicine
keyFacts.value: The NHS says metformin is usually offered first.

keyFacts.label: Common symptoms
keyFacts.value: Tiredness, needing to pee more, constant thirst and unintended weight loss, although many people have none at first.

keyFacts.label: How it is found
keyFacts.value: A GP can usually diagnose it with blood and urine tests.

keyFacts.label: Yearly check-up
keyFacts.value: An annual review covers blood pressure, blood sugar and eye checks, with kidney and foot checks as well.

keyFacts.label: Long-term risks
keyFacts.value: Damage to blood vessels, nerves, eyes, kidneys, feet and gums.

keyFacts.label: Remission
keyFacts.value: Possible for some people; NHS England runs a Path to Remission Programme for eligible people.

keyFacts.label: Emergency route
keyFacts.value: Call 999 or go to A&E for confusion, drowsiness, breathlessness or vomiting with high blood glucose.
